enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal adjournment and permission to appeal
key_facts: Congolese asylum seeker Bosombanguwa sought judicial review after the IAT refused permission to appeal an adjudicator's dismissal of his asylum appeal.
At the adjudicator hearing his expected solicitors did not attend; he claimed he sought an adjournment but the adjudicator recorded that he did not.
Grounds focused on whether the adjudicator should have investigated further before proceeding without representation and whether he suffered prejudice.
Post-hearing medical and other material did not establish that additional evidence would have assisted the claim on the merits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the IAT's refusal of permission to appeal; the court was invited to decide the permission application itself rather than remit.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; the IAT erred in its approach to adjournment and prejudice arguments but the claimant failed to establish unfairness, prejudice, or that an appeal had a real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: At permission stage a tribunal must consider alternatives where there is an arguable dispute about whether an adjournment was sought or about fairness, but establishing arguable adjudicator error on adjournment does not itself satisfy the trigger for granting permission unless facts show real prospect of success on the merits or another compelling reason; solicitor default and Al-Mehdawi principles limit relief based on adviser negligence.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in treating adjournment and prejudice grounds as a bare conflict of evidence
Whether the adjudicator erred in proceeding without further enquiry into expected representation
Whether lack of representation or solicitor failures caused unfairness or prejudice
Which immigration appeal rules governed the adjournment issue

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970

key_facts: Two severely disabled children H and F, cared for by committed parents, challenged Wandsworth's social care assessments.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum JR amendment refused; wasted costs adjourned
key_facts: Afghan asylum seeker Mohebullah obtained permission for JR based on an alleged failure to respond to representations.
The Home Office had in fact responded on 17 October 2003 but the Treasury Solicitor was unaware when permission was granted.
Claimants sought late amendment to challenge a fresh 17 March 2004 decision after prolonged delay and correspondence.
Treasury Solicitor invited withdrawal and warned of wasted costs; claimant's solicitor cited bereavement and counsel absence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive JR could not proceed; court determined amendment application and adjourned wasted costs to a show-cause hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Leave to amend refused as the original permission basis had fallen away and delay was unjustified; wasted costs order not made today but listed for show cause by end of July 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Where permission was granted on a mistaken premise and a fresh decision supersedes the challenged act, amendment should be refused and fresh proceedings pursued; delay of nearly four months without prompt amendment supports refusal; wasted costs may be adjourned where instructing solicitor lacks instructions.
legal_issues: Whether the claim should be amended to challenge the March 2004 decision
Whether delay since March 2004 justified refusing amendment
Whether a wasted costs order should be made against the claimant's solicitors

enrichment.short_title: Secure tenancy possession: false statement and housing benefit

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Waltham Forest sought possession of Mrs Roberts' secure tenancy at 45 Hungerdown on grounds of rent arrears and a knowingly false housing application.
She denied owning property though she jointly owned 143 Westdown Road and received rental income; housing benefit was stopped creating arrears.
The recorder found a deliberate false statement but held the council was not induced and that arrears arose from wrongful benefit refusal.
The authority appealed on inducement and the county court's jurisdiction over housing benefit entitlement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court possession trial where both Schedule 2 grounds were rejected and reasonableness was considered obiter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on grounds 1 and 5; matter remitted to a different county court judge to determine whether it is reasonable to grant possession.
enrichment.ratio: Inducement under ground 5 requires the false statement to have played a real and substantial part in granting the tenancy; material false statements may infer inducement. A county court cannot determine housing benefit entitlement in defence of possession where the prescribed statutory scheme is exclusive; Cotter applies.
legal_issues: Correct test for inducement under Housing Act 1985 Schedule 2 ground 5
Whether the county court could decide housing benefit entitlement as a defence to rent arrears
Whether reasonableness should be remitted given adjourned benefit appeals

enrichment.short_title: Tracktop colourways: unregistered design right and s.51
key_facts: Lambretta designed a retro red-blue-white tracktop with stripes and logos; Teddy Smith allegedly copied the colourways.
Etherton J held UDR could not subsist in mere colourways, s.51 barred copyright, and Teddy Smith copied on the facts.
Appeal concerned subsistence, s.51 defence, commonplace design, copying finding on French rib evidence, and costs.
Jacob LJ dismissed; Mance LJ dissented on s.51; Sedley LJ agreed with Jacob LJ.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Etherton J on law; Teddy Smith cross-appeal on commonplace and copying.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; UDR held not to subsist in colourways as shape/configuration or as excluded surface decoration; s.51 bars copyright claim; design commonplace if necessary; copying finding would not stand but liability fails on subsistence.
enrichment.ratio: Mere juxtaposition of colourways on a standard garment is not 'shape or configuration' for UDR and is excluded as surface decoration; s.51 prevents enforcing artistic copyright in industrial design documents for non-artistic articles; 'commonplace' compares designs in a broad design field relevant to designers.

enrichment.short_title: Pupillage application not membership of chambers
key_facts: Disabled mature student Horton was offered pupillage at 1 Pump Court but could not start due to ill health.
Chambers refused deferral to October 2002; he claimed disability discrimination under section 13 DDA.
Employment tribunal held chambers a trade organisation and pupillage an application for membership; EAT reversed on membership.
Court split 2-1: Peter Gibson and Parker LJJ dismissed; Laddie J would have allowed, holding pupils are members.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from EAT on statutory construction of membership of a trade organisation under section 13 DDA.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted but appeal dismissed; applying for pupillage is not an application for membership of barristers' chambers within section 13.
enrichment.ratio: Member and membership under section 13(4) must be read in context of a trade organisation whose members carry on the profession; a pupil is a trainee without governance rights and Bar Code para 803 prohibits pupils becoming members; specific pupillage provisions in sex and race discrimination Acts suggest Parliament did not treat pupillage as section 13 membership.

Whether an application for pupillage is an application for membership

enrichment.short_title: Gypsy homelessness: bricks and mortar B&B offer

statutes_considered.title: Caravans Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Romany gypsy Mrs Codona and extended family lived in caravans on unlawful Plot 7 at Woodside Caravan Park near Sandy.
After planning enforcement and injunctions the council accepted homelessness duty but offered conventional bed and breakfast accommodation.
Mrs Codona had a strong aversion to bricks and mortar housing and sought pitches for six or seven caravans together.
No lawful council or private gypsy site was available at short notice; council could only offer temporary B&B pending longer-term housing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 204 Housing Act 1996 from county court upholding section 202 review of suitability of offered accommodation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; temporary bed and breakfast could be suitable suitable accommodation despite cultural aversion where no caravan pitch available, subject to Article 8 balancing and duration limits.
enrichment.ratio: Suitability under sections 193 and 206 is fact-sensitive and includes nature, location, condition and duration; duty is absolute but bounded by Wednesbury minimum standards; gypsies warrant special consideration under Chapman but Article 8 does not require provision of caravan sites and bricks and mortar may be offered as last resort if above minimum suitability.
legal_issues: Whether bed and breakfast bricks and mortar accommodation can be suitable for a gypsy with cultural aversion to conventional housing
Role of council resources and availability of land
Application of Article 8 and Article 14 ECHR
Whether an empty caravan pitch constitutes accommodation under section 193

enrichment.short_title: Cream spill: vicarious water pollution conviction
key_facts: About 10 litres of cream spilled at Express Ltd's Redditch depot when Pardy's Dairies employee Wassell's grundy toppled during transfer.
Some cream entered surface drains and discoloured Hewell Brook for 150-200 metres with increased BOD and suspended solids.
Pardy's pleaded guilty to section 85(1); Express was convicted under section 217(3) as the act or default causing that offence.
Express permitted daily cream transfers on a slope near drains without adequate spill or pollution risk assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Redditch magistrates convicting Express Ltd under section 217(3) following Pardy's section 85 offence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; all five case stated questions answered in the affirmative; Express's defaults sufficiently caused Pardy's pollution and cream was polluting matter despite no proven harm.
enrichment.ratio: Section 217(3) requires an act or default of another person due to which the primary section 85 offence is committed; a landowner permitting a hazardous operation without risk assessment may be liable when pollution occurs; polluting matter under section 85 need not cause actual harm if it taints or has polluting effect per Dovermoss.
legal_issues: Whether Express's act or default caused Pardy's section 85 offence under section 217(3)
Whether cream was polluting matter without proof of environmental harm
Whether loading operations at a retail depot could be a positive causative act
Whether absence of a written risk assessment could constitute default

enrichment.short_title: Administration moratorium: PPA construction claim refused
key_facts: AES Barry Ltd operated a Barry power station under a gas supply PPA with TXU Europe Energy Trading.
TXU entered administration in November 2002; early termination notice crystallised a disputed early termination payment exceeding £60 million.
AES sought permission under section 11(3) to commence Commercial Court proceedings on PPA construction issues before a scheme of arrangement.
Administrators held over £1 billion for creditors and proposed scheme machinery including expert determination, court access, interim dividends and interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to commence proceedings against company in administration under section 11(3) Insolvency Act 1986.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; moratorium not lifted because AES could prove claim through scheme with interim dividend, interest, and later court or expert resolution; AES ordered to pay costs with £50,000 interim payment pending detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Permission under section 11(3) requires the applicant to make out a case; for monetary claims the moratorium preserves assets and orderly administration—creditors should normally use scheme or administration machinery unless inequitable to prohibit proceedings; no sufficient prejudice where scheme will allow interim payment on undisputed sums, interest, and court determination if needed.
legal_issues: Whether to lift the section 11 moratorium for PPA construction litigation
Balancing creditor prejudice against orderly administration and scheme approval
Whether Commercial Court proceedings would pre-empt scheme claim resolution
Costs of the one-day application and interim payment on account
